agency-ad-report-automation:
Every Monday at 8 AM, this workflow pulls last week's numbers from Meta Ads, Google Ads, and GA4 in parallel, blends them into spend, clicks, impressions, conversions, revenue, ROAS, CTR, and CPA, has an AI analyst write a plain-language client summary, emails a branded HTML report to the client, and drops a digest in the agency's Telegram. Every stage is logged to Google Sheets (**RUN_STARTED** → **DATA_FETCHED** → **SUMMARY_GENERATED** → **REPORT_SENT**). It is built for small agencies and freelancers whose Monday mornings disappear into screenshots and spreadsheet math.

### The 3-person agency with 12 retainer clients

A boutique paid-media shop runs ads for a dozen local and DTC clients, and each account manager burns three hours every Monday pulling numbers into a slide deck. With this template, the **Weekly Monday 8AM Trigger** fires once and the three pull nodes (**Meta Ads — Pull Insights**, **Google Ads — Pull GAQL**, **GA4 — Pull Conversions**) run in parallel. **Merge — Ads Platforms** and **Merge — All Channels** combine the responses, **Compute Totals** blends everything, and **AI Agent — Write Ad Summary** (gpt-4o-mini with **Structured Output Parser — Summary**) returns a standout metric, a risk, a recommendation, and a 60-second summary. **Build Report HTML** assembles the branded email using the brand color from **CONFIG — Report**, **Gmail — Send Client Report** delivers it, and **Telegram — Run Digest** posts the totals plus the AI take to the team. Practical variation: keep a Clients sheet with names, IDs, and emails, and wrap the flow in a Split In Batches loop so a single Monday run reports for every retainer client.

### The solo freelancer defending retainer value

A freelance media buyer manages seven accounts and constantly fields the question "what am I paying for?" from clients who never log into ad dashboards. The Sheets audit trail is the answer: the Report Log tab shows **RUN_STARTED** through **REPORT_SENT**, proving the report went out on schedule every week. More valuable is the structured AI output: the **risk** field surfaces a creeping CPA and the **recommendation** field gives the freelancer a concrete talking point for the monthly call. **CONFIG — Report** holds client name, client email, and brand color per copy, so each client gets a report that looks made just for them. Practical tip: store each week's totals in a second sheet tab and add a Code node computing week-over-week spend and ROAS deltas before the AI step — the summary gets noticeably sharper with a trend to react to.

### The in-house marketer reporting to a non-technical founder

A sole marketer at a DTC brand spends Friday afternoons translating dashboards for a founder who ignores every chart. The plain-language 60-second summary from **AI Agent — Write Ad Summary** is the whole product: one paragraph the founder will actually read, anchored by a standout metric and one recommendation. **Build Report HTML** renders it in a branded layout so it reads like a briefing, not a spreadsheet. For TikTok or LinkedIn spend, duplicate one HTTP pull node, extend **Compute Totals** with the new platform's fields, and add a row to the report table. Practical tip: set the lookback window in **CONFIG — Report** to 30 days once a month for a monthly rollup edition without building a second workflow.

### The lead-gen agency that needs early warnings

A lead-gen agency for home-services businesses once discovered broken conversion tracking three weeks late, after the client had already noticed. Two features of this workflow exist for exactly that failure mode. First, **IF — Any Data?** verifies at least one platform returned rows; empty data takes the failure branch — **Sheets — Log REPORT_FAILED** records it and **Telegram — Failure Alert** pings the team — so a silent miss never happens. Second, the AI's **risk** field is prompted to flag anomalies like sudden conversion drops. Practical variation: add an extra condition that treats zero conversions as a failure even when spend data exists, so a tracking break triggers the alert branch instead of a cheerful report about impressions.

### The consultant packaging reporting as a productized service

A marketing consultant wants to sell "weekly ad reporting" as a fixed-price add-on without hiring anyone. This template is the delivery mechanism: import one copy per client, fill in **CONFIG — Report** and the six **CONFIG — API Access** placeholders, and the service runs itself. For clients who file reports, add an HTML-to-PDF step between **Build Report HTML** and Gmail so the email carries an attachment. If the team lives in Slack rather than Telegram, swap the two Telegram nodes for Slack nodes — the digest text works unchanged. Practical tip: the client Q&A customization (a Gmail Trigger plus a second AI agent answering replies from the same week's data) turns the report into an interactive deliverable worth charging more for.
ai-content-repurposer:
This workflow turns one video or podcast transcript into roughly twenty platform-native pieces: an X thread, a LinkedIn post, a Facebook post, an Instagram caption, a newsletter section, quote cards, Shorts and Reels scripts, and a blog summary. You paste the transcript into **CONFIG — Content Source** along with your brand voice and target audience, and **AI Agent — Repurpose Content** (gpt-4o-mini, guided by **Structured Output Parser — Content Plan**) writes every piece in that voice, for that audience, with no invented facts. Each piece becomes its own row in Google Sheets, the run is tracked **NEW** to **PROCESSING** to **DONE**, and **Telegram — Repurposing Complete** sends per-platform counts. It is built for creators and small teams who record once and then watch the content die on a hard drive because repurposing takes longer than recording.

### The solo podcaster with a back catalog

A podcaster has sixty published episodes and a social feed that goes quiet between recordings, because turning one episode into posts takes two evenings she does not have. She pastes an episode transcript into **CONFIG — Content Source**, sets the brand voice once, and runs the workflow manually. **Sheets — Log Source NEW** records the episode, **Split Output Per Platform** turns the structured output into one item per post, **Sheets — Log Content Items** appends each row, and **Build Completion Summary** counts pieces per platform for the Telegram digest. One 30-minute transcript costs roughly three cents per run, so repurposing the whole back catalog costs less than a coffee. Practical variation: swap the Manual Trigger for a Schedule Trigger that reads the week's newest transcript from a Content Queue sheet, turning the back catalog into a self-draining pipeline.

### The 2-person coaching business turning webinars into a pipeline

Two coaches run a weekly live webinar that gets watched once and forgotten, while their email list and social accounts starve. The newsletter section and quote cards are the highest-value outputs for them: the newsletter section feeds the list, the quote cards feed stories, and the LinkedIn post positions the coaches as practitioners. Because the AI writes in the configured brand voice rather than generic marketing speak, the pieces sound like the coaches, not a bot. Practical tip: use the human review gate customization — change the Status the content items log with from **PROCESSING** to **NEEDS_REVIEW**, and only flip rows to **DONE** after editing. For a coaching brand where tone is the product, ten minutes of review beats full automation.

### The YouTuber expanding onto LinkedIn and a newsletter

A creator with a solid YouTube audience wants to be on LinkedIn and run a newsletter, but rewriting every video is a second job. The **linkedin_post**, **blog_summary**, and **newsletter_section** outputs solve exactly this: same ideas, native format, no invented facts. The **platforms_to_generate** list in **CONFIG — Content Source** lets her generate only the three formats she publishes, skipping the rest. Practical variation: add a Whisper transcription step before the config so pasting a video URL is all she needs — no manual transcript copy-paste, and the **IF — Transcript Not Empty** guard still catches blank runs before any API calls are wasted.

### The agency repurposing client interview footage

A three-person content agency records monthly founder interviews for retainer clients, and the approval bottleneck is the agency owner reading every draft. The Google Sheet becomes the approval queue: each row is one piece with its own Content cell, ready to copy. The **NEEDS_REVIEW** status variation from the customize guide fits perfectly — the strategist reviews rows, the client sees only approved ones. The per-platform split also makes scope visible: the client can literally count the twenty deliverables. Practical tip: keep a Platforms sheet (platform, enabled) and add an IF per format before **Split Output Per Platform**, so a client who only publishes on LinkedIn and X gets exactly those outputs billed cleanly.

### The course creator feeding a launch

A course creator launches in six weeks and needs thirty days of content without stopping course production. She runs one workflow execution per module transcript: the **shorts_scripts** become teaser clips, the **x_thread** outputs become launch threads, and the **blog_summary** becomes SEO pages that keep working after launch. The **source_title** in the config keeps every run labeled by module, so the sheet doubles as a launch content inventory. Long transcripts are truncated to 500 characters only in the source-log row — the AI still sees the full text, so nothing is lost. Practical tip: add an X node after **Split Output Per Platform** that posts items with Content Type **x_tweet** in order, turning the digest into a genuine publish pipeline for launch week.
ai-devotional-reels-factory:
Send a deity or scene photo with a caption idea to a Telegram bot, and this workflow builds a cinematic devotional reel end to end. The photo is pulled from Telegram, archived to Google Drive, and logged in Sheets with status **RECEIVED**. **OpenAI Vision: Analyze Photo** produces a structured YAML description so every later step stays faithful to the reference. An agent writes the NanoBanana keyframe prompt, fal.ai renders the keyframe, **AI Agent: Generate Reel Script** outputs a VEO3-ready JSON prompt covering camera, lighting, motion, VFX, and audio, and kie.ai's VEO3 renders the 9:16 vertical video with polling waits until it is ready. **Rewrite Caption with GPT-4o** writes a reverent Devanagari caption under 150 characters with bhakti hashtags, and Blotato publishes to Instagram, YouTube Shorts, TikTok, Facebook, and X in parallel before the sheet flips to **Published** and a Telegram confirmation arrives. It is built for devotional creators and temple teams who want daily cinematic reels without an editing desk.

### The temple trust posting daily darshan reels

A temple trust's media volunteer is expected to post a reel every morning, but he has no editing skills and a full-time job. His new workflow is taking one photo at the temple and sending it to the bot with a caption idea like "morning aarti diyas." The pipeline handles the rest: keyframe, script, VEO3 render, Hindi caption, five-platform publish. The **Google Sheets: Log Idea** tracker, with its **STATUS** column moving from **RECEIVED** to **Published**, gives the trust committee a visible content calendar without anyone asking for reports. Practical variation: add the posting-schedule customization — a Schedule Trigger branch that reads **READY** rows from the sheet and posts at fixed times — so festival-day reels queue up instead of publishing the instant they render.

### The solo devotional creator running five platforms from a phone

A creator with eighty thousand followers was reformatting and uploading the same video five times, losing an hour a day to busywork. The **Upload Video to BLOTATO** step plus the five Blotato platform nodes (Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Twitter/X) merged back together publish everywhere from a single upload, and **Telegram: Send Published Notification** confirms it landed. Her entire production loop is now: photograph, caption idea, wait, confirm. Practical tip: insert the approval customization — a Wait or Telegram approval step between **Send Final Reel Preview** and **Upload Video to BLOTATO** — so nothing goes public before she has seen the final render on her phone.

### The spiritual publisher mining a photo archive

A publisher sits on ten thousand festival photographs that have never been used for video. The archive path is the **Google Drive: Upload Photo** node paired with the tracker sheet's **IMAGE URL** and **IMAGE DESCRIPTION** columns: every photo becomes a catalogued asset, and **OpenAI Vision: Analyze Photo** writes the structured description (subject, colors, setting, mood) that keeps the NanoBanana keyframe faithful to the original scene rather than drifting into generic imagery. Each archived photo can then be re-run through the reel pipeline on festival anniversaries. Practical variation: edit the **Format Prompt** code node to change **aspectRatio** to 16:9 for YouTube-style landscape versions of the same reels.

### The bhakti community manager with zero video skills

A community manager for a 40,000-member devotional group was asked to "do reels" with no budget and no editor. Her technical ceiling is sending a Telegram message, which is exactly the workflow's input: photo plus a caption idea in plain words. The **Generate Image Prompt** agent translates her simple idea into the devotional keyframe language (diya glow, marigold tones, cinematic realism) she could never write herself. Practical tip: if her audience reads Hinglish better than pure Hindi, edit the prompt in **Rewrite Caption with GPT-4o** to write Hinglish captions instead — one prompt change, every future reel follows.

### The overseas devotee page keeping festivals alive

A diaspora-run page wants to post through every major festival but its admins are spread across three time zones and keep missing days. The workflow's structure solves the coordination problem: anyone can send a photo idea to the bot at any hour, the **Wait for VEO3 Rendering** node handles the slow render step without babysitting, and the sheet's **URL VIDEO FINAL** column keeps every finished reel in one place for resharing next year. Practical variation: duplicate any Blotato platform node, pick Pinterest or Threads, and wire it into the **Merge** node (raising Number of inputs to match) to reach the diaspora audiences that live on those platforms.
ai-guest-messaging-vacation-rentals:
This is an always-on messaging desk for a vacation-rental business. A **Guest Message Webhook** receives inbound guest messages — a channel manager or PMS like Hostaway, Lodgify, or Guesty forwards Airbnb and Booking.com threads to it, and email arrives through an IMAP-to-webhook bridge. **Normalize Guest Message** unifies every payload, the message is logged with status **NEW**, and **AI Agent — Classify & Draft** reads it against the property context (check-in and check-out times, WiFi password, house rules) and returns a structured verdict through **Structured Output Parser — Guest Intent**: intent, confidence from 0 to 1, an **auto_reply_allowed** flag, a ready-to-send draft reply, and an escalation reason. **IF — Safe to Auto-Reply?** passes only when auto-reply is allowed and confidence meets the threshold (default 0.85): the draft goes out via **Send Guest Reply**, the sheet flips to **AUTO_REPLIED**, and the host gets a Telegram summary. Anything else — refunds, complaints, access codes, safety issues, or low confidence — flips to **ESCALATED** and fires the **Telegram — Escalate to Host** alert with the guest's message, the AI's read, the reason, and a suggested draft. It exists because slow replies cost stars, and 2 AM WiFi-password questions cost sleep.

### The 15-property Airbnb host losing evenings to check-in questions

A host with fifteen listings spends two hours every evening answering the same five questions: WiFi password, check-in time, parking, checkout, house rules. Those map exactly onto the default **safe_intents** list (wifi, checkin, checkout, houserules, amenities, parking, directions), and the answers live in **CONFIG — Properties & Rules** — checkin_time, checkout_time, wifi_password, house_rules_url — so the AI drafts from facts, not guesses. With the confidence threshold at 0.85, the routine questions get answered in seconds while anything ambiguous escalates. Practical tip: extend the system prompt with a per-property facts block (gate codes, parking spots, quiet hours) keyed off the **property** field from **Normalize Guest Message**, so a fifteen-property setup still answers precisely.

### The co-host managing 30 listings who needs sleep

A co-host's response-time metric directly affects search ranking, but she cannot answer messages at 3 AM. The auto-reply branch is her night shift: **Send Guest Reply** POSTs the draft to the PMS reply endpoint, **Update Sheet — Status AUTO_REPLIED** records it, and **Telegram — Notify Host (Auto-replied)** gives her a morning summary of who got what answer. She wakes up to a log instead of a backlog. Practical tip: raise the **confidence_threshold** to 0.9 or higher in **CONFIG — Properties & Rules** — with thirty listings, she would rather escalate a borderline message than risk a wrong auto-reply at scale.

### The boutique villa with strict house rules

A luxury villa owner keeps finding extra guests and late-night parties because the rules were buried in a PDF nobody read. The **houserules** intent plus the **house_rules_url** in config means every rules question gets an instant, consistent answer with the link — no more improvised replies from whoever happened to see the message. Early check-in and late checkout requests intentionally escalate, since those are revenue decisions, not FAQ answers. Practical tip: use the third-branch customization — extend the parser's intent list with **upsell** and route airport transfers and paid late checkouts to a human draft, turning escalations into revenue instead of chores.

### The property manager who will not risk refunds going wrong

A manager with twenty doors refuses to let any software touch money conversations. The workflow agrees with her: **refund** and **complaint** intents never pass **IF — Safe to Auto-Reply?**, and the escalation alert includes the guest's message, the AI's interpretation, the escalation reason, and a suggested draft, so she replies in one minute instead of ten. The **Draft Reply** column in the sheet stores everything the AI ever sent, giving her a weekly audit trail. Practical tip: during the first two weeks, disconnect the true branch of the IF node into escalation entirely — calibrate on real messages, watch the confidence scores, and only reconnect auto-reply once the scores earn her trust.

### The glamping operator with patchy connectivity

A rural glamping host is often offline for hours, which used to mean guests waited half a day for simple answers. Now the webhook, the AI agent, and the auto-reply branch run without her: routine questions resolve themselves, and the **Telegram — Escalate to Host** messages queue on her phone for the moment she has signal. The sheet's **NEW** to **PROCESSING** to **AUTO_REPLIED** or **ESCALATED** trail means she can reconstruct the whole day in five minutes. Practical tip: pre-filter obvious OTA auto-messages (booking confirmations) with an extra IF on message keywords before the agent runs, so the AI — and the API bill — only touches messages from real humans.
ai-job-hunt-automator:
A daily job-hunting assistant that runs every morning while you sleep. The **Daily 9AM Trigger** fires **Search Jobs — JSearch API** (RapidAPI, aggregating Google Jobs) with the keywords and location from **CONFIG — Job Search**. **Normalize Job Listings** standardizes each posting, **Read Seen Job URLs** plus **Filter New Jobs Only** drop anything already processed, and new postings are logged with status **NEW**. **AI Agent — Score Resume Match** compares each job against the resume text and returns a structured score from 0 to 100, a verdict from **STRONG_MATCH** to **NO_MATCH**, top strengths, and key gaps via **Structured Output Parser — Match Score**. The sheet flips to **SCORED**; jobs at or above the threshold pass **IF — Score ≥ Threshold** (default 70), get a tailored cover letter of max 250 words referencing real achievements from **AI Agent — Write Cover Letter**, saved to Google Docs, and the sheet flips to **COVER_LETTER_READY**. Both branches merge into **Build Daily Digest**, and **Telegram — Send Digest** delivers the count of new jobs plus strong matches with direct apply links. It deliberately stops before applying — auto-submitting can violate job board terms, so the workflow prepares everything and you click apply.

### The laid-off software engineer running a full-time search

An engineer laid off in a restructuring is treating the search as a job, but scrolling job boards for three hours a day is not a system. With **max_results** at 20 and keywords like "backend engineer," the workflow scans, dedupes, and scores every morning; the Telegram digest tells him there were 14 new postings, 3 strong matches, and here are the apply links with cover letters already sitting in Google Docs. The **Key Gaps** column doubles as interview prep — he can see exactly which required skills he lacks before the recruiter call. Practical tip: raise **match_threshold** to 80 once the pipeline is full, so the digest only surfaces roles worth the application effort.

### The career switcher testing new waters

A support engineer wants to move into AI engineering but does not know which postings are realistic. The verdict scale (**STRONG_MATCH** down to **NO_MATCH**) plus the strengths and gaps output turns each morning's digest into market feedback: after two weeks she can see which of her skills transfer and which gaps repeat. The resume text in **CONFIG — AI Scoring** is the lever — she rewrites it to emphasize projects, and the scores move. Practical tip: lower the threshold to 60 while exploring. At the exploration stage, borderline matches are information, not noise.

### The final-year student running a structured hunt

A student applying to forty companies keeps everything in memory and loses track of who replied. The sheet's status flow — **NEW** to **SCORED** to **COVER_LETTER_READY** — is already a pipeline; adding **Applied**, **Interview**, and **Rejected** columns (per the customize guide) turns it into a full tracker with zero extra tooling. The dedupe logic (**Read Seen Job URLs** plus **Filter New Jobs Only**) means reposted jobs never clutter the list, which matters when campus season reposts the same roles weekly. Practical tip: if JSearch coverage is thin for her market, swap the search node for the Adzuna API — only the **Normalize Job Listings** code node needs remapping.

### The employed job seeker with fifteen minutes a day

A working professional cannot job-hunt at a desk all day; she has the train ride. The digest design fits that constraint exactly: one Telegram message with the day's strong matches and apply links, cover letters already written and saved. She reads the digest, opens the top two matches, clicks apply, done. Because the workflow never auto-applies, there is no risk of an accidental application to her current employer's posting — she sees everything first. Practical tip: change the Schedule Trigger to weekly if the daily cadence produces more digest than she can act on; the dedupe logic keeps any cadence safe.

### The remote-only job seeker filtering out the noise

A designer who will only work remotely was drowning in "hybrid, three days in office" postings. Setting **location** to Remote in **CONFIG — Job Search** filters at the source, and the AI scoring then ranks what remains against the resume rather than the commute. The digest becomes a short list of genuinely applicable roles instead of a long list of maybes. Practical tip: for very high volumes, add an IF filter before scoring that only scores jobs from target companies — scoring is the expensive step, and gpt-4o-mini is cheap but not free.
ai-lead-capture-enrich-score-crm:
A ten-node pipeline that stops every website form fill from getting equal attention. **Lead Webhook** captures the lead's name, email, company, and company domain. **Enrich Company** fetches firmographics — size, industry, location — from an enrichment provider. **Score Lead**, a GPT agent, weighs the enriched data against the ideal customer profile described in its system prompt and returns a JSON score plus a one-line reason. **Parse Score** extracts the number into clean fields, clamped to 0–100 so routing stays deterministic. **IF Hot Lead** checks the threshold of 70: hot leads land in the **Hot Leads** tab of Google Sheets and trigger a **Slack Alert** with score, reason, and contact details; everything else files into the **Nurture** tab for later campaigns. It exists for the team that calls every lead in order and wonders why the good ones went cold.

### The B2B SaaS founder qualifying trial signups

A founder gets twenty trial signups a day and cannot personally reach out to all of them, so she reaches out to none of them systematically. The **Slack Alert** changes the dynamic: a message with the lead's name, company, score, and the one-line reason arrives the moment a hot lead signs up, and she replies while the signup is still warm. The ideal customer profile lives in the **Score Lead** system prompt — company size, industry, geography — so "hot" means her definition, not a generic one. Practical tip: edit the **IF Hot Lead** threshold to match how she actually defines hot; a founder with a high-touch sales motion might set it at 80 and treat the 70s as nurture.

### The agency qualifying contact-form inquiries

A five-person agency gets a mix of serious briefs and tire-kickers through the same contact form, and the partners waste discovery calls on both. Enrichment plus scoring sorts them before the first call: a 200-person company in the agency's core vertical scores high with a reason like "mid-size SaaS, hiring signal in industry," while a solo blog scores low and files to **Nurture**. The one-line reason is the key feature — it tells the partner *why* in the Slack message, not just a number. Practical tip: follow the customize guide and swap the Google Sheets nodes for HubSpot, Salesforce, or Pipedrive nodes, so hot leads land directly in the pipeline the sales team already works in.

### The sales team racing speed-to-lead

Three SDRs know that responding within five minutes multiplies conversion, but the old process batched leads into a spreadsheet someone checked twice a day. The webhook-to-Slack path collapses that to seconds: form submit, enrich, score, alert. The SDR who claims the alert first works the lead, and the **Hot Leads** tab keeps the record straight. Because **Parse Score** clamps and cleans the number, the routing never misfires on a malformed model response. Practical tip: chain a second HTTP request after **Enrich Company** to pull technographic or funding data before scoring — a lead running a competitor's tool or fresh off a funding round is a hotter conversation.

### The fractional SDR prioritizing outreach lists

A fractional SDR inherits a 500-row list from a client's last campaign and has ten hours a week. Scoring the list through the webhook turns it into a ranked call sheet: the top of the **Hot Leads** tab gets the calls, the **Nurture** tab feeds the email sequence. The enrichment step matters most here, because stale lists have the thinnest data and firmographics fill the gaps. Practical tip: rewrite the scoring criteria in **Score Lead** per campaign — the ICP for an enterprise push and a mid-market push are different, and the prompt is the cheapest thing in the workflow to change.

### The consulting firm scoring RFP inquiries

A consultancy spends days on proposals, so a bad-fit RFP is expensive, not just annoying. The score plus the one-line reason gives the partners a fast, defensible triage: pursue, nurture, or decline with a polite template. Lower-scoring inquiries are not discarded — the **Nurture** tab keeps them for the quarterly check-in campaign, which is where consulting pipelines quietly come from. Practical tip: when proposal cost is high, raise the threshold above 70 and tighten the ICP description in the prompt; the workflow's value is in what it keeps *out* of the proposal queue.
ai-meeting-notes-tasks:
Drop a meeting transcript into a Google Drive folder and this workflow turns it into tasks. **New Transcript Arrived** (a Drive trigger polling every 5 minutes) fires, **Download Transcript** fetches the file, and **Extract Transcript Text** decodes it — .txt and .md supported, long transcripts truncated at around 12,000 characters with a note. **AI Agent — Extract Action Items** reads the transcript and, via **Structured Output Parser — Action Items**, returns a meeting summary plus an action-items array, each with a task title, owner, due date in YYYY-MM-DD, and priority of high, medium, or low; items with no named owner fall back to the configured default owner. **Split Action Items** fans them out, **Notion — Create Task** writes each one into the Notion Tasks database (Name, Owner, Due, Priority, Source), **Log Task — CREATED** appends it to the Meeting Tasks sheet, **Build Slack Summary** aggregates everything into one numbered list with owner, due date, and priority, **Slack — Post Meeting Summary** posts it to the channel, and **Telegram — Notify — Tasks Created** confirms the count with the top three. The sheet tracks **EXTRACTED** to **CREATED**. It exists because "who was supposed to do that?" is the most expensive question in any company.

### The 6-person agency turning client calls into task lists

An agency's client calls end with verbal commitments that scatter across chat threads and memory, and the Monday status meeting becomes archaeology. Now the call transcript — from Fireflies, Otter.ai, or Whisper, saved as .txt — goes into the watched Drive folder, and within minutes the tasks sit in Notion with owners, due dates, and the meeting file recorded in the **Source** field. The Slack summary in the client channel means the client sees the same task list the agency sees, which ends most "I thought you were doing that" disputes before they start. Practical tip: use the per-team routing customization — duplicate the Notion node and add an IF on the file name (standup versus sales-call) to route tasks into different databases per team or client.

### The founder doing ten user interviews a week

A founder running customer discovery generates ten transcripts a week and reads none of them twice. The **meeting_summary** from the structured output is the executive layer she actually consumes, while the extracted action items capture every "I'll send you the deck" and "let me intro you to" promise before it evaporates. The Meeting Tasks sheet becomes a searchable log of every commitment made across all interviews. Practical tip: add a Google Drive move node after extraction to file processed transcripts into an Archive folder — the watched folder stays clean, and the archive becomes a research corpus.

### The remote team's async standups

A distributed team across four time zones records a fifteen-minute async standup daily, but nobody watches all of them. The transcript goes in the folder; the **Slack — Post Meeting Summary** message in #meetings is what everyone actually reads — a numbered list of who is doing what by when, with priorities. The **default_owner** in **CONFIG — Task Routing** catches the vague "someone should..." items and assigns them to the team lead instead of letting them float. Practical tip: map owners to Slack user IDs and extend the plain-JS summary builder with mention formatting, so assignees get pinged directly in the summary message.

### The consultant who bills on decisions

A consultant's scope disputes always come down to what was agreed on which call. Every task the workflow creates carries the **Source** field pointing at the meeting file, and the sheet logs date, file, task, owner, due date, and priority with status **CREATED** — a paper trail built automatically. When a client questions a deliverable, the consultant pulls the row, not a memory. Practical tip: add the human-in-the-loop customization — an n8n Wait node before **Notion — Create Task** — so nothing enters the official task system until the consultant has reviewed the extraction. For billable work, a two-minute review is cheap insurance.

### The ops manager routing onboarding tasks

An ops manager runs onboarding calls that generate a dozen small tasks — accounts to create, docs to send, intros to make — and half of them slip. The workflow catches them all, and items where the AI cannot identify an owner fall back to the ops manager herself via **default_owner**, which is exactly right: unowned onboarding tasks are her job until delegated. Practical tip: if the transcription tool can POST directly, use the webhook alternative from the setup guide — delete the three Drive nodes, add a Webhook node, and have the tool POST the file name, transcript text, and meeting date. The rest of the chain works unchanged.
ai-resume-screening:
A hiring pipeline that reads every application. **Gmail Trigger** watches the inbox and fires on new application emails — the filter is yours to set, for example subject contains "application." **Download Resume** grabs the attachment, **Parse Resume with AI** has GPT read it and return clean structured JSON (name, email, skills, years of experience, a short summary), and the **Job Description** Set node holds the job posting you paste in once. **Score Candidate** compares the parsed resume against that JD and returns a 0–100 score plus strengths and risks; **Normalize Result** tidies everything into clean fields; **Append to Sheet** adds one ranked row per candidate to Google Sheets, highest scores on top when sorted. **High Score?** continues only at 80 or above, and **Create Interview Draft** creates a Gmail *draft* interview invite — a human reviews and sends every invite, because the workflow never emails anyone automatically. It exists for the hiring manager who reads the first twenty applications and ignores the other one hundred eighty.

### The startup founder hiring the first engineers

A founder posts a backend role and gets 150 applications with no HR team and no ATS. The ranked sheet is the whole shortlist process: sort by score, read the top fifteen summaries, check the **risks** column for red flags like job-hopping or missing core skills. The **strengths** field tells her why each candidate scored well, so she is not trusting a bare number. Because the **Job Description** node holds the actual posting, the scoring is anchored to what she asked for, not a generic "good engineer" judgment. Practical tip: edit the system prompt in **Score Candidate** to weight skills, experience, or education differently — for a first engineering hire, she might weight demonstrated shipping experience above credentials.

### The 5-person agency hiring an intern

An agency needs a design intern, gets 90 applications, and the partners cannot justify a week of resume reading. The default 80 threshold is too strict for an intern role, so they open **High Score?** and lower the cutoff — the workflow's value here is the ranked sheet and the parsed summaries, not the interview gate. The draft invite text in **Create Interview Draft** gets rewritten in the agency's casual voice, and it still stays a draft until a partner hits send. Practical tip: keep the threshold modest and let the **risks** column do the filtering — for junior roles, a clear, honest resume often matters more than a high score.

### The recruiter running five roles at once

A solo recruiter is hiring a frontend dev, a PM, a designer, and two sales reps, and candidates keep landing in the wrong pile. The fix is one copy of the workflow per role: each copy gets its own **Job Description** node, its own Gmail filter (subject contains "frontend application" versus "PM application"), and its own sheet tab. Applications sort themselves by role, score themselves against the right JD, and rank themselves. Practical tip: for PDF resumes, add an Extract from File node between **Download Resume** and **Parse Resume with AI**, and point the parsing prompt at its extracted text — scanned or image-based PDFs otherwise parse poorly.

### The retail chain hiring seasonal staff

A retail ops manager needs forty seasonal hires in two weeks and receives 500 applications across three stores. Speed is the entire game: the workflow parses and scores overnight, and the morning sheet is a ranked list per store. The **summary** field lets her scan a candidate in ten seconds, and the **risks** field flags the obvious mismatches. She lowers the **High Score?** threshold for volume roles — the interview itself is the real filter at this scale, and the workflow's job is just to order the queue sensibly. Practical tip: sort the sheet by score descending and work top-down; the normalize step keeps every row in identical shape, so the sheet stays scannable at 500 rows.

### The non-technical founder screening developers

A non-technical founder cannot tell a strong React resume from a padded one, which used to mean either reading everything anxiously or delegating blindly. The parsed **skills** and **years of experience** fields give her structured facts, the **summary** gives her a plain-language read, and the score measures fit against the JD her technical advisor helped write. She reviews the ranked sheet, reads the top summaries, and personally sends the interview invites from the drafts — the human-in-the-loop design means the workflow advises but never acts on her behalf. Practical tip: have the technical advisor review the **Job Description** node text once — the entire scoring quality flows from how precise that posting is.
ai-stock-reports:
A four-workflow multi-agent system that produces institutional-style stock research every week. The main orchestrator runs on a **Schedule Trigger** every Monday at 06:20, loops over a 15-ticker watchlist with **Loop Over Items**, and a form trigger ("Manual Entry: Stock Analysis") allows on-demand analysis of any single ticker. Each ticker is fed through **Execute Workflow** into an **AI Agent** on the Google Gemini chat model, which must call all three sub-workflow tools in order — **Technical Analysis Tool**, then **Trends Analysis Tool**, then **Fundamental Analysis Tool** — and synthesizes everything into a strict JSON report: recommendation, sentiment counts, chart URL, technical write-up, top articles, hot topics. The technical sub-workflow validates the ticker via TwelveData, pulls 180 days of price history with Bollinger Bands and MACD, renders a TradingView chart image via Chart-IMG, computes Fibonacci levels and support/resistance in a Code node, and has GPT-4o Vision read the chart. The fundamental sub-workflow pulls company Overview, Income Statement, and Balance Sheet from Alpha Vantage (with 12-second waits between calls to respect rate limits) and extracts MarketCap, P/E, EPS, and two-year revenue and net-income trends. The trends sub-workflow fetches Alpha Vantage news sentiment and counts bullish, neutral, and bearish articles with hot-topic ranking. Back in the main workflow, if the recommendation title contains "Buy," a $7,000 paper buy order fires on Alpaca; **Generate HTML** renders the report into a styled email, **Adjust HTML Colors** recolors sections by sentiment, and **Send Stock Analysis** emails it via SMTP. These are research aids for study and decision support, not financial advice — and the buy branch can be removed to keep the system reports-only.

### The retail investor's Monday watchlist review

An investor tracking fifteen US stocks used to spend Sunday evenings assembling research from five websites. The Monday 06:20 run does it while he sleeps: by breakfast, one styled HTML email covers all fifteen tickers with the same structure — technicals, fundamentals, news sentiment, recommendation. The sentiment-colored sections from **Adjust HTML Colors** let him triage visually before reading a word. Practical tip: edit the **tickers** array in the **Stock List** node — any NASDAQ or NYSE symbols work, and the TwelveData validation step rejects bad tickers before they waste API calls.

### The investment club's shared research desk

An eight-member investment club argues from different data every month because everyone researches differently. The strict JSON report schema fixes that: every ticker gets the same sections, the same sentiment counts, the same structure, so the club debates conclusions instead of data. The **top articles** and **hot topics** fields give the meeting its discussion agenda. Because the sub-workflows are separate imported files called as tools, the club's technically inclined member can improve the technical analysis once and every future report benefits. Practical tip: move the **Schedule Trigger** to Sunday evening so the reports are waiting when the club meets Monday night.

### The finance newsletter writer's research assistant

A newsletter author covering markets needs a research draft per stock without spending a day per stock. The form trigger is her tool: type a ticker into "Manual Entry: Stock Analysis" and get the full three-agent report on demand, with the **technical write-up** and **top articles** sections serving as the draft's backbone. She rewrites in her own voice — the workflow is a research starting point, not publishable copy. Practical tip: delete or deactivate the **Buy?** to **Buy in Alpaca** branch. A writer has no use for paper orders, and reports-only mode keeps the workflow simpler and cheaper to run.

### The paper trader testing strategy ideas

A swing trader wants to test whether acting on the agent's recommendations would have worked, without risking money. The Alpaca integration already points at Alpaca's paper API: when the recommendation title contains "Buy," **Buy in Alpaca** places a $7,000 notional paper order, creating a real track record of the strategy's calls. The **notional** value is editable to match his actual position sizing. Practical tip: tighten the **Buy?** condition — for example, also require the overall sentiment to be Bullish — so the paper portfolio only acts on high-conviction calls, which is the version of the strategy worth evaluating.

### The finance student learning real analysis

A finance student finds textbooks abstract and real analyst reports opaque. Watching this system work teaches the structure of equity research: the agent must call technical, then trends, then fundamental analysis, mirroring how professionals triangulate price action, news flow, and financials. The Fibonacci and support/resistance Code node shows how levels are computed, not just asserted, and the sentiment-colored HTML makes the relationship between news tone and recommendation visible. Practical tip: use the "swap the brain" customization — point the **Google Gemini Chat Model** at different Gemini models and compare how the recommendations change, which is itself a lesson in model sensitivity.
ai-video-generation-autopublish:
A weekly video pipeline with a human gate in the middle. The **Schedule Trigger** starts it every Monday at 9:00 AM. **Set Topic** defines the video's topic and target audience for the run. **OpenAI: Write Script** sends the topic to GPT and gets back a ready-to-render 60-second video script. **HTTP Request: Render Video** POSTs the script to a video-generation API (HeyGen or Synthesia style) and gets back a video URL. **Gmail: Request Approval** emails the finished video link plus an approval link — and this is the load-bearing step: nothing publishes until a human approves. **Wait: Human Approval** pauses the execution; opening the approval link from the email shows an Approve/Reject form built from the execution's resume URL, and submitting it resumes the workflow exactly where it paused. **IF: Approved?** routes approved videos to **HTTP Request: Publish to Socials** (posting to the X/LinkedIn scheduler) and **Slack: Notify Published**; rejections go to **Slack: Notify Held**. It exists for people whose video ideas die because production always feels like a project.

### The solo founder's weekly product tip

A SaaS founder knows a weekly 60-second tip video would build her audience, but filming, editing, and uploading never survive contact with her calendar. Her Monday loop is now: edit **Set Topic** to this week's tip (or leave a rotating list), let the 9 AM run write the script and render the video, and approve from the Gmail on her phone over coffee. The approval email carries the video link, so she watches the actual render before it goes anywhere — quality control without a production day. Practical tip: feed topics from a Google Sheet instead of the **Set Topic** node, so a quarter of topics can be planned in one sitting and the pipeline never stalls waiting for an idea.

### The course creator's promo clips

A course creator needs eight weeks of launch promos and dreads recording eight videos. With a Synthesia-style avatar as presenter, each week's run turns a module highlight into a polished 60-second clip: the script comes from GPT, the render from the video API, and her only job is the approval click. The **Slack: Notify Published** message gives her team a visible record of what went out each week, which matters when a launch has five people coordinating. Practical tip: duplicate **HTTP Request: Publish to Socials** and point the copy at a second scheduler endpoint — one approval then publishes to both X and LinkedIn without extra work.

### The local business's weekly offer video

A gym owner wants a short video every week announcing the week's class schedule and offers, but hiring a videographer weekly is absurd for a single location. The topic each Monday is simply this week's offer; the render is template-consistent, which is actually a branding advantage — followers recognize the format. Approval happens on his phone between sessions, and **Slack: Notify Held** tells his part-time social media helper when a video was rejected so she knows to expect a re-run, not a post. Practical tip: change the cron expression in the **Schedule Trigger** (currently Monday 9 AM) to whatever day the week's offers are finalized — the pipeline fits the business rhythm, not the other way around.

### The agency producing client content with approval built in

A three-person agency promised clients "two videos a month" and the approval process is chaos: cuts sent over WhatsApp, feedback in email threads, nobody sure which version is final. This workflow makes approval structural instead of social. The **Gmail: Request Approval** email goes to the client directly, the Approve/Reject form is unambiguous, and the workflow physically cannot publish a rejected video — **IF: Approved?** enforces it. **Slack: Notify Held** alerts the agency the moment a client rejects, with no chasing required. Practical tip: resist the "auto-publish without approval" customization for client work. Deleting the **Wait** and **IF** nodes is only sensible for the agency's own channels, where it trusts its own taste.

### The newsletter writer going video

A writer with a 20,000-subscriber newsletter wants to repurpose each issue as a short video but has no on-camera presence and no editor. Each week she pastes the issue's core angle into **Set Topic**; **OpenAI: Write Script** compresses it into a 60-second script; the avatar video carries it. The approval step doubles as her editorial check — she watches the render the way she would proofread a draft. Over a quarter, the video catalog becomes a discovery surface that points back at the newsletter. Practical tip: once the pipeline has earned her trust after a month of approvals, consider the auto-publish customization — but keep the Gmail notification, so she still sees every video that went out.
ai-voice-agent-lead-calling:
Every minute between a form submission and your first contact costs you the deal. This template is for businesses that collect inbound leads — through a website form, a booking page, or a CRM — but can't call back fast enough. The **Lead Webhook** receives the lead the moment it's submitted, **Normalize Fields** cleans the phone number into a dialable format, and an AI agent called **Qualify Lead** reads the notes and returns a strict JSON verdict: qualified or not, plus a one-line reason. Qualified leads trigger an AI voice call through your provider (Vapi, Twilio, or similar), the workflow then books a follow-up on your Google Calendar via **Book Calendar Event**, and **Notify Team** posts who was called, when the follow-up is, and why they qualified to Slack. Everyone else gets a *nurture* tag via **Tag Nurture** so they're filed for later instead of forgotten.

### Home services company with a flood of quote requests

A roofing or HVAC company getting 20–30 quote requests a day usually loses half of them to a competitor who called first. Wire your website's quote form to the **Lead Webhook** and the workflow calls back within a minute — no dispatcher needed. **Qualify Lead** reads the notes field ("roof leaking in two spots, needs quote this week" vs. "just browsing prices") and only real intent fires the **Trigger Voice Call** request, so you're not paying for calls to tire-kickers. The calendar booking defaults to *tomorrow at 10:00 UTC*; adjust the event logic in **Book Calendar Event** to your timezone and crew availability. Variation: start conservative — insert a Wait node between **IF Qualified** and **Trigger Voice Call** so your office manager approves each call before it dials, then remove the gate once you trust the AI's judgment.

### Real estate agency working nights and weekends

Listing inquiries arrive at 11 PM, but the agent on call is showing a house. With this workflow live, a late-night inquiry gets an instant qualification check and an AI voice call while the buyer is still on their couch scrolling. Edit the system prompt in **Qualify Lead** to add your real criteria — budget range, preferred neighborhoods, pre-approval status — so renters get tagged *nurture* instead of burning call credits. The **Notify Team** Slack post tells the morning agent exactly who was called, when the follow-up event is, and why the lead qualified, so the handoff is seamless. Tip: tighten the call script parameters in **Trigger Voice Call** to offer a specific viewing slot ("I have Thursday 4 PM or Friday 11 AM") — two choices convert better than an open-ended "when works for you?"

### B2B agency chasing demo requests

A 10-person agency gets demo requests from its site but half are students doing research or vendors selling something. **Qualify Lead** acts as your bouncer: tune its system prompt with company size, industry, and role criteria, and only real prospects reach **Trigger Voice Call**. For auditability, add a Google Sheets node after **Parse Decision** to log every lead, verdict, and reason — after a week you'll see which sources send the best leads and can sharpen the prompt. Practical tip: the **Normalize Fields** step strips non-dialable characters from phone numbers, but it can't fix a wrong country code, so make your form require a country picker up front.

### SaaS company following up on free-trial signups

Trial users who never activate are the easiest revenue to recover. POST each new signup to the **Lead Webhook**, and **Qualify Lead** can score intent from signup data — company size, team seats invited, features clicked — all stuffed into the notes field. Qualified signups get a voice call offering a 15-minute onboarding session, and **Book Calendar Event** drops it straight on the rep's calendar while the prospect is still thinking about the product. Because the flow is fully automatic, one rep can cover the trial volume that used to need three. Variation: swap the fixed scheduling for a round-robin across your sales team by editing the calendar logic, so the follow-up lands with whoever is on shift.

### Local clinic or consultancy filling its consultation diary

A physiotherapy clinic or financial advisor lives on booked consultations, and inbound inquiries often sit in an inbox for hours. This workflow turns each inquiry into a call and a booked slot within minutes. **Book Calendar Event** sends the invite through the Google Calendar API with the client attached, and the Slack notification keeps the front desk in the loop without anyone watching the form. Unqualified inquiries (outside your service area, wrong service type) are tagged *nurture* automatically — revisit them later with an educational email series instead of losing them.
appointment-waitlist-backfill:
Every cancellation is revenue evaporating. This template is your 24/7 receptionist for freed appointment slots: your booking system POSTs the cancellation to the **Webhook — Cancellation Intake**, the workflow scores your waitlist deterministically in **Code — Score & Rank Waitlist** (days waiting × your weight, minus a no-show penalty, plus loyalty and priority-flag bonuses), logs the top candidates as *RANKED*, and an AI agent writes a warm, personalized offer message for each. The messages go out through the **HTTP — Send Offer (Demo Provider)** node to your WhatsApp or SMS provider with a "Reply TAKE within 120 minutes" instruction appended, rows flip to *OFFER_SENT*, and the **Wait — Reply Window** pause starts. Replies come back through the **Webhook — Reply Intake**, get matched to the latest open offer in **Code — Match Reply to Offer**, and it's first TAKE wins — the winner flips to *BOOKED*, everyone else flips to *EXPIRED*.

### Dental clinic losing money on hygiene cancellations

A 3-dentist clinic sees 4–6 hygiene cancellations a week, and each empty 45-minute slot costs around $150. Wire your booking software to POST cancellations to the waitlist-cancel webhook with `appointment_id`, `slot_time`, and `service`. Patients on your Waitlist tab get scored automatically — long waiters float up, chronic no-shows sink — and the top 3 get the AI-written WhatsApp offer within seconds of the cancellation. The first reply of TAKE books the slot, the rest are expired automatically. Practical tip: set `reply_window_minutes` to 30 for same-day slots so the sweep in **Sheets — Mark EXPIRED** closes fast and you can try a second wave of candidates if the first wave stays silent.

### Salon or spa filling same-day gaps

Salons know that a Thursday afternoon cancellation can still be filled if you act within the hour. Set `offer_count` to 3 in **CONFIG — Waitlist Rules** and let the **AI Agent — Write Offer Copy** (gpt-4o-mini with structured output) write offers that feel personal — mentioning the service, the stylist, the time — rather than a robotic blast. The deterministic reply keyword `TAKE` keeps the matching in **Code — Match Reply to Offer** reliable: no fuzzy parsing, no confusion. Variation: if you don't want the OpenAI call, delete the AI Agent and its two sub-nodes and connect **Sheets — Log Ranked (RANKED)** straight to **Code — Build Offer Message** — the fallback template message still gets the slot filled. And if two clients reply TAKE in the same minute, only the first match wins; the other offer expires, and your Telegram alert shows you exactly who replied.

### Physiotherapy or medical practice with chronic no-shows

No-show penalties are built into the scoring on purpose. A clinic that flags repeat no-shows in the `No Shows` column automatically pushes them down the ranking, so your scarce freed slots go to reliable patients first — fairness you can defend to anyone who asks. Service matching means candidates only get offers for their service type (blank matches any), so a physio cancellation never gets offered to a podiatry waitlist by accident. Tip: raise `weight_wait_day` so the longest-waiting patient always wins the tie — in healthcare, perceived fairness matters as much as speed, and the score column in the Offers tab gives you an auditable record of *why* each person was chosen.

### Auto service center or grooming studio with repeat regulars

A car service center or dog groomer lives on loyal repeat customers — exactly what the `Visits` column rewards. Crank `weight_visit_loyalty` in the config and your regulars get first dibs on cancelled Saturday slots, which is precisely the loyalty gesture that keeps them coming back. The full status flow in Sheets — *NEW* → *RANKED* → *OFFER_SENT* → *BOOKED* / *EXPIRED* — means at the end of the month you can count exactly how many slots you recovered and what they're worth. Practical variation: build the escalation ladder from the guide — offer candidate #1, wait 30 minutes, and only then offer candidate #2 — if you'd rather fill one slot reliably than race three candidates against each other.

### Owner who wants oversight without being the bottleneck

You never have to watch the sheet. **Telegram — Owner: Offers Sent** tells you who got contacted, **Telegram — Owner: Window Closed** confirms the sweep finished, **Telegram — Owner: Slot Booked** names the winner, and **Telegram — Owner: Unmatched Reply** flags messages that matched no open offer (a mistyped keyword, a question about a different appointment) so you or your staff can handle them personally. Tip: while testing, keep the reply window short (15–30 minutes), because the cancellation webhook's response waits for the window to close in `lastNode` mode — long windows make testing painfully slow.
client-onboarding-orchestrator:
New-client onboarding is a chain of small tasks that's easy to drop a link of: the Notion project, the Drive folder, the Slack channel, the welcome email, the kickoff call. This template turns one webhook POST into the whole chain. Your CRM, form, or checkout POSTs `name`, `email`, and `company` to **Webhook — New Client**; the workflow slugifies the company name, appends a *RECEIVED* row to your Clients sheet, then provisions everything — a Notion project page via **Notion — Create Project Page**, a Google Drive folder under your parent folder via **Drive — Create Client Folder**, and a `client-<slug>` Slack channel with a welcome post tagging you. The sheet flips to *PROVISIONED*, Gmail sends the welcome email, **Code — Compute Kickoff Date** schedules the kickoff N days out at 10:00 for 45 minutes on Google Calendar, and the sheet flips to *WELCOMED*.

### Marketing agency signing retainers weekly

A 6-person agency signs 2–3 retainers a month, and each one currently costs the founder an hour of setup busywork. Point your proposal tool or checkout at the webhook and every new client gets identical, instant setup: their `client-acme-corp` channel opens with links to their Notion project page and Drive folder, the welcome email lands with what-happens-next and the timeline, and the kickoff call is already on both calendars three days out. The 🎉 Telegram summary confirms the happy path; the Slack failure alert with the error message tells you exactly which step broke if something does. Practical tip: change `kickoff_days_ahead` in **CONFIG — Business** if your process is faster — a high-velocity agency might use 1 day, a strategy consultancy 5.

### IT consultancy where every client needs a project space

An IT or software consultancy lives inside client workspaces — project pages, shared folders, comms channels — and inconsistency between clients creates confusion for months. This workflow makes every client space identical: same Notion page structure, same Drive folder location, same channel naming convention from the **Code — Slugify Company** step. Every provisioning node runs with `onError: continueErrorOutput`, so a Drive hiccup doesn't kill the Slack channel — the flow jumps to the STEP 4 alert chain, posts the failure to your alerts channel with the client name and error, and flips the sheet to *FAILED* for a clean retry. Variation: switch the Slack scope to `groups:write` and set `isPrivate: true` if client channels should be private — the welcome post and failure alerts work the same either way.

### Fractional CFO, coach, or consultant with a personal process

Solo practitioners feel onboarding overhead most — there is no ops person to hand it to. For a coach with 15 active clients, the webhook can fire from a simple form on the website: the welcome email goes out with the timeline and contact details, the kickoff event lands on the `primary` calendar (changeable in **Calendar — Create Kickoff Event**), and the Clients sheet gives a one-glance pipeline of who is *RECEIVED*, *PROVISIONED*, *WELCOMED*, or *FAILED*. The Clients sheet columns — Date, Name, Email, Company, Notion Page, Drive Folder, Slack Channel, Status — become your lightweight CRM for the first 30 days of every relationship. Tip: put a true Slack @mention in the welcome post by hardcoding your user ID as `<@U12345678>` so new clients actually see it in the channel.

### Law firm or financial practice with a contract step

Regulated practices usually need a signed engagement letter before the kickoff. The guide's customize section fits here: insert a DocuSign or PandaDoc node between the welcome email and the kickoff event, add a `Contract` column to the sheet, and the status flow gains a natural pause — the row stays *PROVISIONED* until the contract is signed. The **Slack — Alert Owner (Step Failed)** chain means a failed document send doesn't leave a client stranded between steps; you see the failure in `#general` (or your own alerts channel) with the error message and can intervene. Because the whole flow is driven by config and sheet updates, adding this step doesn't disturb the Notion/Drive/Slack provisioning that already ran.

### Agency owner who wants a client list that maintains itself

Skip the CRM complexity: the four Sheets nodes (*RECEIVED* append, *PROVISIONED*, *WELCOMED*, *FAILED* updates, matched on Email) keep one Clients tab that is always current. If you outgrow Sheets, the guide notes the values map 1:1 to CRM pipeline stages, so swapping the four Sheets nodes for your CRM's create/update nodes is mechanical. Practical variation: don't need Drive folders? Delete the node and remove its reference from the PROVISIONED update — the error chain reroutes automatically and nothing else changes.
cold-email-outreach-automation:
Cold email still works — but only if every email feels written for its recipient and your sending stays disciplined. This template runs one daily campaign from a Google Sheet: **Daily Outreach Timer** fires at 9:00 AM, **Read Unsent Leads** pulls leads with `status=unsent` (capped at about 20 a day), and **Process Leads One-by-One** loops through them. For each lead, **Write First Line (AI)** writes a 1–2 sentence personalized opener from the lead's name, role, company, and recent activity, **Compose Email** builds the full message with your one-click unsubscribe link, and **Send Email** sends it via Gmail. **Wait 90 Seconds** paces the sends inside Gmail's rate limits, **Mark Lead Sent** flips the status, and the loop continues. A separate **Unsubscribe Webhook** chain receives opt-out clicks and **Mark Opted Out** flips those leads to `opted-out` so they're never emailed again.

### Lead-gen agency running outreach for clients

A 3-person agency running outbound for five clients needs personalization at scale without a copywriter per account. Each client gets their own sheet tab; the AI opener references the lead's role, company, and `recent_post` column, so "noticed your team just launched the Berlin office" lands in every email without manual research. The 20-a-day cap and 90-second waits keep each client's Gmail account safe — and if a client wants more volume, you spin up a second Gmail sender rather than pushing one account past its limits. Practical tip: add `industry` and `pain_point` columns and reference them in the **Write First Line (AI)** prompt; the deeper the inputs, the less the opener sounds like a template.

### SaaS founder doing founder-led sales

A founder emailing 20 prospects a day personally can't also run the company. This workflow sends at 9 AM while you have coffee: every email carries a genuinely personal first line, the unsubscribe link keeps you compliant, and — critically — the workflow never auto-replies to responses, so any reply lands in your inbox for a human to handle. Start with the guide's compliance note taken seriously: only email people you have the right to contact, and make the unsubscribe link work without a login. Variation: add a Gmail Trigger chain that flags replies in Slack so you respond within hours instead of discovering them at day's end — the guide suggests this as the single highest-leverage addition.

### Recruiter sourcing passive candidates

Recruiters email engineers who get five recruiter emails a week — the generic ones get deleted. With a `recent_post` column capturing a candidate's recent talk, open-source release, or job move, the AI opener references something real: "saw your post on migrating to event-driven architecture" beats "I came across your profile" every time. The loop node means each candidate still gets full personalization even at 20 a day, and **Mark Lead Sent** plus the sheet status columns give you a clean record of who was contacted and when — no double-emailing candidates across months. Tip: for hard-to-fill roles, slow the pace deliberately (edit the 90-second **Wait** upward) and raise the quality bar in the opener prompt instead of raising volume.

### Freelance designer or copywriter pitching studios

A freelancer pitching 100 studios over a month needs consistency more than volume. Queue all 100 rows with `status=unsent`, cap the daily sends, and let the workflow drip them out over five days while you do billable work. The **Compose Email** template is fully editable — write it in your own voice, show one line of proof (a result, a link), and keep the ask to a 15-minute call. The **Unsubscribe Webhook** chain handles opt-outs automatically, which matters when you're emailing cold: one-click unsubscribe that actually works keeps your domain reputation clean and keeps you on the right side of CAN-SPAM and GDPR. Practical variation: segment by `role` — studio founders get one email angle, marketing heads another — by filtering rows before each run.

### Consultant testing two offers side by side

Because the email template lives in one node, A/B testing is simple: duplicate the workflow, change the subject line and opener angle in **Compose Email** in each copy, and point them at two halves of your sheet. After two weeks, compare reply rates in your inbox — the sheet's `sent` timestamps let you line up cohorts exactly. The per-lead loop through **Process Leads One-by-One** guarantees both variants get identical personalization quality, so the test measures the offer, not the opener. Tip: never test deliverability factors (send time, volume) at the same time as message factors — change one variable, hold the other constant, and give each test at least 100 leads before judging.
competitor-price-monitoring:
Pricing moves fast and manual checking doesn't scale. This template watches competitor product pages every day: **Daily Schedule** fires at 09:00, **Read Products** pulls your rows (`product_name`, `url`, `last_price`) from Google Sheets, and **Fetch Product Page** downloads each page once. **Extract Price** pulls the price out of the HTML with a CSS selector you set per site, **Normalize Price** strips currency symbols into a plain number, and the **Price Changed?** IF node compares the live price against `last_price`. On a change, **Send Price Alert** messages you on Telegram — "Price changed: X was $A, now $B" with the product link — and **Update Last Price** writes the new price back so tomorrow's run compares against it. Adding products is just adding rows; the workflow itself never needs to change.

### Small ecommerce brand defending its margins

A DTC brand selling a $60 skincare set against two competitors can't afford to be 20% overpriced for a month without noticing. Add each competitor's product URL as a row, set the CSS selector in **Extract Price** (right-click the price → Inspect → copy selector), and every morning you either get silence or a Telegram alert with the exact before-and-after. When a competitor drops to $47, you see it the same day and can decide — match, hold, or differentiate — instead of discovering it in a quarterly review. Practical tip: change the **Price Changed?** condition from "not equals" to "smaller than" so you only get pinged on price *drops*, which are the moves that actually threaten your sales.

### Dropshipper or reseller protecting their spread

Resellers live on the gap between their cost and the market price. Track the supplier listings and the main competitor listings in the same sheet; when a supplier raises a price, the Telegram alert tells you to adjust your listing price the same morning instead of selling at a loss for days. Because the workflow writes the new price back into the sheet every run, you also build a free price-history dataset — after three months you can see each supplier's discount rhythm and time your own promotions around it. gmail-ai-auto-labeling-triage:
Your inbox is a to-do list written by other people, and reading all of it costs an hour a day. This template triages Gmail with AI in two independent chains. Chain 1 is instant: **Gmail Trigger: New Email** fires on every new message (polling each minute), **OpenAI: Classify Email** reads the subject and snippet and classifies it into exactly one category — `urgent`, `action`, `fyi`, or `spam` — and the **Switch: Route by Category** node sends it down one of four branches, each ending in a **Gmail: Apply Label** node that stamps the matching label. Chain 2 is the morning briefing: **Schedule Trigger: Daily Digest** fires at 8:00 AM, **Gmail: Fetch Labeled Unread** pulls unread urgent and action emails from the last day, **OpenAI: Summarize Digest** turns them into a short plain-English digest with one line per email, and **Gmail: Send Digest** emails it to you.

### Founder getting 200 emails a day

A founder's inbox mixes investor updates, customer fires, newsletters, and noise — and the important email is always buried. With instant labeling, the *Urgent* label becomes the only inbox view that matters during the day: a customer outage email lands labeled Urgent within a minute of arrival, while newsletters quietly collect under FYI. The 8 AM digest means you start the day with a one-line-per-email summary of everything urgent or action-worthy from the last 24 hours instead of re-reading the inbox. Practical tip: add an alert node after **Gmail: Apply Label — Urgent** — a Slack or Telegram ping the moment something urgent arrives — so truly critical mail interrupts you even when you're not looking at email.

### Customer support lead watching for escalations

A support lead needs to know about the angry enterprise customer *before* the ticket ages out. Tune the classification prompt in **OpenAI: Classify Email** so that escalation language, SLA keywords, and key-account domains count as *urgent*, and the label becomes an early-warning system: the support manager's *Urgent* view is a real-time escalation queue. The digest gives the Monday-morning picture of what the weekend left behind. Variation: rename the categories to match support workflows — edit the prompt and the Switch branches together (for example `escalation`, `refund-request`, `feature-ask`, `noise`) so labels map to your actual queue semantics.

### Real estate investor juggling deals and contractors

An investor's email is deal flow, contractor quotes, property-manager updates, and spam in equal measure. The four default categories map well: deal emails with deadlines become *urgent*, quotes needing a decision become *action*, market newsletters become *fyi*, and the junk self-filters to *spam*. The daily digest replaces the evening inbox sweep — one email, one line per item, decisions queued for the morning. Because classification reads the subject and snippet, set up a filter habit: the AI can only classify what it sees, so keep subject lines meaningful in the mail you *send* (contractors will mirror them in replies). Tip: the digest query in **Gmail: Fetch Labeled Unread** already limits itself to urgent and action — adjust the `q` filter if you want FYI items included on weekends when you do deeper reading.

### Freelancer separating money mail from noise

A freelancer's income depends on two email types: client work and invoices — everything else can wait. With triage running, the *Action* label collects the emails that need a reply or a deliverable, and the digest makes sure nothing urgent from a client slips past a busy week. Newsletters and cold pitches land in FYI or Spam without ever demanding attention. The customize path is easy: edit the prompt to add categories like `receipts` or `prospect`, rename the Switch branches and labels to match, and your bookkeeping mail self-organizes. Practical variation: change the digest time in **Schedule Trigger: Daily Digest** — a freelancer who works nights might prefer the digest at 10 PM as a next-day prep instead of 8 AM.

### Agency owner with a team inbox to supervise

An agency owner doesn't read every client email — but needs to know when one is on fire. Point the workflow at the shared client-services inbox: *urgent* labels surface the "we're considering leaving" email within a minute, the digest gives the owner a daily one-line brief without opening the inbox, and the *action* label shows the account manager's real to-do list. The classification prompt can be tuned with client names and project codenames so the AI weighs context correctly. Tip: start with the four default labels for two weeks, then review what landed where — the misclassifications tell you exactly which phrases to add to the prompt, and one prompt edit improves every future email.
invoice-ar-chaser:

A startup's first finance hire needs audit trails, not spreadsheets-by-email. Practical variation: connect a Gmail send node after **Google Sheets: Mark Rejected** to notify the vendor automatically — the rejection reason can ride along, closing the loop instead of leaving the vendor guessing.

An ecommerce brand's payables are supplier invoices, freight bills, and agency retainers — high volume, mixed formats. The AI extraction shines here because supplier invoices rarely share a layout: the model reads vendor, amount, date, and invoice number regardless of template, which is exactly what breaks brittle template-based parsers. Set the approval threshold to match your delegation policy — maybe $500 for a lean team — and everything above it waits for the founder's tap. The sheet becomes the month-end close input: filter by *reconciled* and *auto-reconciled* for the booked payables, investigate the *pending* stragglers. Tip: review the extracted amounts for your first 20 invoices against the PDFs; the one field AI occasionally misreads is the total when invoices show subtotals and tax prominently — a quick spot-check habit beats a painful month-end surprise.

Agency owners often approve every invoice personally because they don't trust the process — which doesn't scale past a dozen vendors.
